transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-12
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Sanjay Rao (Cobalt Head of ML), Jessica Morales (Cobalt Infra Lead), Ethan Park (Cobalt CTO)
Recording ID: ff-2025-11-12-cobalt-poc-001

Summary:
Quick scoping call to define POC success criteria, baseline workload sizing, reserved GPU choices, burst strategy and fallback policies; agree timeline and benchmark plan.

Topics:
- Workload characteristics (req/s, tokens/request, peaks)
- Reserved capacity vs hosted burst pools
- Autoscale triggers, cool-downs, pre-warm strategies
- Fallback policies (model variants, region failover)
- Success criteria and timeline for 2-week POC

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick check we got the right folks on the line?
[00:08] Sanjay: Yep this is Sanjay, we got Jessica and Ethan on the call too. Good to meet you Maya, Liam.
[00:12] Maya: great thanks, i'll hand over to Liam to run through the technical scoping, i'll chime on pricing and timeline.
[00:18] Liam: cool thanks. So high level for the POC we're trying to scope capacity — reserved GPUs, burst and fallback. Sanjay can you run us through your current traffic and what you want to validate?
[00:30] Sanjay: sure. Right now our prod approximation, we're seeing about 15k active users with an average 0.7 reqs/user/day but there's big variance — some internal workflows hit spikes. Typical request size ~150 tokens input, 250 tokens output so ~400 tokens total on average. Peak we need to be able to handle short bursts up to ~220 requests/sec for 2-3 minutes. Sustained during day is more like 40-60 req/s.
[00:57] Jessica: to add, our infra team wants to lock down VPC egress and ensure KMS integration, and we'd prefer a dedicated pool for the POC to isolate results.
[01:10] Liam: ok that helps. For 400 tokens per request at 220 rps peak, that's ~88k tokens/sec peak — which is heavy. For the POC we typically recommend starting with a dedicated H100 for transformer models or 2x A10G depending on the model and quantization. do you have a target latency SLO?
[01:36] Sanjay: p95 under 250ms for the top-tier flows, p50 should be under 120ms. We understand some long-tail prompts will be slower, but those are lower priority.
[01:47] Maya: just to be explicit on success criteria — throughput to meet peak with p95 <250ms, no more than 1% error rate, and a short benchmark report with cost per 1M tokens. also a short quality check vs your baseline model outputs.
[02:05] Ethan: sounds fair. For cost we want ballpark numbers, we don't need final pricing but something to compare against OpenAI.
[02:13] Liam: we'll include that. Now on autoscaling, does Cobalt want reactive autoscale (add GPUs on demand) or a reserved plus burst model?
[02:22] Jessica: prefer reserved for baseline to keep latency predictable, but allow bursts from a shared pool to handle spikes. also we need defined fallback — if burst pool exhausted, fallback to smaller model or region.
[02:35] Liam: that's our typical pattern: reserved x GPUs for baseline + burst capacity we can pull from cross-tenant burst pools (or dedicated burst if you prefer) and fallback chain where we degrade to a quantized model or smaller model variant, and finally rate-limit. We'll discuss policy order.
[02:49] Sanjay: important that fallback doesn't catastrophically change results; quality checks should detect regressions.
[02:55] Maya: yes we'll tie fallback to a quality threshold — if smaller model drops below agreed metric we won't automatically switch for critical flows.

[03:10] [Speaker 1]: (brief noise)

[03:25] Liam: ok let's do some numbers — if we set baseline reserved at 1x H100, that typically supports roughly 60-80 rps for a 30B model depending on batching and quantization, 2x A10G might be similar but with different cost profile. for your peak of 220 rps we'd recommend reserved 2x H100 or 1x H100 + burst pool sized for the remaining spike.
[03:55] Jessica: budget wise, we can commit to 1x H100 as reserved; need to see cost delta for adding a second. can you also show burst pricing?
[04:04] Maya: yes we'll send a capacity worksheet with cost scenarios: reserved only, reserved + burst shared, reserved + dedicated burst. Also include estimated token cost per 1M tokens.
[04:13] Sanjay: how do you handle pre-warming and cold-starts for cached KV? we need low latency for first request after idle.
[04:22] Liam: two approaches: keep a small number of warm workers pinned (pre-warm) and use prefix/KV cache to avoid recompute for repeated contexts. There's also an option to keep warm idle pods and spin-up thresholds tuned to your traffic pattern. For POC we can configure a small pre-warm pool.
[04:36] Ethan: what's the fallback chain you'd propose? smaller model, quantized variant, region failover, then throttling?
[04:43] Liam: yes order would be: 1) same model quantized (e.g., int8) on same hardware if available, 2) fallback to a smaller architecture we validated for quality, 3) route to another region with capacity if cross-region acceptable, 4) rate-limit gracefully with informative error payload.
[05:00] Jessica: okay. Can we set SLOs per route? ex: critical route gets no fallback to smaller model unless manual approval.
[05:08] Maya: yes Redwood supports per-route rollout policies and can pin that route to only use premium model and skip automatic downgrade — we'll document how to configure that.

[05:30] Liam: for benchmarking, we want two waves: baseline steady-state 30-60 rps for 1 hour, then spike tests: 220 rps for 5 min, then sustained 120 rps for 30 min, plus noise tests with sudden bursts. We'll run with your sample prompts to measure p50/p95/p99 and error rates.
[05:50] Sanjay: that works. Are you able to run heavy token workloads? some of our flows have 1k+ tokens occasionally.
[05:58] Liam: yes long-context evaluation will be part of the run. we'll also test KV/prefix caching impact on tail latency.

[06:20] [00:06:20] Jessica: transcription note: we're going to need the firewall egress IPs for the POC.

[06:30] Maya: we'll include those in the security pack. we'll also share our SOC2 artifact link and KMS integration doc.

[07:00] Liam: on autoscale policy specifics — typical settings: scale up when average GPU utilization > 60% for 30s, scale up step 1 GPU, cool-down 120s, scale down when utilization < 30% for 120s; pre-warm a single worker when predicted spike over threshold. But these are tunable.
[07:26] Sanjay: makes sense. for our burst pattern the short 2-3 minute spikes might be missed if we wait 30s — is there event-based quick scale?
[07:35] Liam: yes we can use request rate triggers in addition to GPU utilization — if request rate > X for Y seconds, we pre-warm extra capacity immediately. that's the burst strategy for short spikes.
[07:45] Ethan: any risk of thrashing with very spiky traffic? we don't want to oscillate GPUs.
[07:51] Liam: avoid thrash with cooldowns and predictive pre-warm; also use a small buffer of reserved burst capacity so short spikes are absorbed. We'll show a policy recommendation.

[08:15] Maya: a note on metrics we'll deliver: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, batching sizes, model switching events, error rates, cost per 1M tokens. We'll also attach model output diffs for quality checks.

[08:40] [00:08:40] Sanjay: on model selection — we'll test your recommended open model (redwood-optimized) and also run our internal baseline. important to know how quantization affects quality.

[09:00] Liam: yep we'll run multiple profiles: fp16 baseline, int8 quantized, and a smaller distilled variant. each will have throughput/latency/cost numbers plus a small eval set for quality.

[09:20] Jessica: timeline — we want this POC to be about two weeks. Week 1: env setup and baseline tests; Week 2: spike tests, fallback validation, and final report. Is that feasible?
[09:31] Maya: that's our suggested plan. we can start provisioning as soon as we get the traffic samples and access. we'll aim to deliver final report within 3 business days after bench runs.

[09:50] Liam: about environment access — we'll need service account details, VPC peering options, and a list of endpoints to allow. Jessica if you can share the infra gating items we'll prepare a checklist.
[10:02] Jessica: i'll send the infra checklist today; also we'll want the test harness to support replay of production traces (sanitized).

[10:12] Liam: fine, we'll make harness that can replay traces with token-level pacing. also will include loadgen scripts and a small synthetic set to simulate spikes.

[10:30] [00:10:30] Sanjay: how are you measuring cost? token accounting, GPU hours, and infra overhead?

[10:38] Maya: yes we report token-based cost plus GPU time and network egress where relevant. for Reno — sorry Redwood — we'll show both per 1M tokens and per-hour GPU cost for the exact config used.

[11:00] Liam: one more technical detail — KV cache warm-up: if many unique sessions you'll see lower cache hit rate; we'll report cache hit vs latency and show recommendations for prefix caching strategies.

[11:18] Ethan: any limitations with your private deployment path? we might need on-prem later.

[11:24] Maya: Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem packaging; POC can be on hosted/dedicated, and if you need on-prem later that’s a separate engagement. For evaluation we'll focus on hosted dedicated instance.

[11:40] [00:11:40] Liam: regarding fallback quality gating — we'll compute BLEU/ROUGE-ish diffs for generation where applicable and a small manual evaluation for critical intents. fallback only triggers for non-critical routes unless you opt-in.

[12:05] Jessica: good. can you also provide a suggested autoscale policy file we can preview and tune?

[12:12] Liam: yes we'll attach a recommended policy with thresholds and explainers.

[12:30] Maya: ok let's capture next steps and action items.
[12:36] Sanjay: before we close one risk: if burst pool is multi-tenant will noisy neighbors affect our p95?
[12:42] Liam: burst pools are isolated by scheduling and we conservatively cap allocation; we can offer dedicated burst capacity for the POC if you want full isolation.

[12:55] Ethan: we probably want dedicated burst for the POC to get clean numbers.
[13:00] Maya: noted, we'll propose dedicated burst option in the worksheet.

[13:20] [00:13:20] Jessica: final question — who will run the actual benchmark? Redwood or Cobalt?
[13:25] Maya: Redwood can run it jointly; we'll provide the harness and run with your team present. we'll share raw logs and dashboards.

[13:40] Liam: OK that gives us enough to prepare a detailed POC plan. I'll summarize required inputs: traffic samples, evaluation prompts, infra access, and any routes that should be protected from automatic fallback.

[14:00] Sanjay: we'll get that to you by EOD Friday.

[14:10] Maya: perfect. recap on timeline: 2025-11-14 capacity worksheet + sizing, 2025-11-17 benchmark scripts ready, run benchmarks 2025-11-18 to 2025-11-20 window, final report by 2025-11-24.

[14:35] Jessica: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[14:40] Ethan: thanks.
[14:42] Maya: thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark and the security packet.

[14:50] [00:14:50] End of recording

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard acronyms (e.g., K V cache transcribed as "K V cash"), speaker turns may be off by a second, filler words kept in.
